Feature: pass^k reliability readout + adaptive run-count recommendation
Pain point: A single pass hides whether the agent behaves the same way twice; users ship agents that passed once and fail unpredictably
Source dates: reliability paper 2026-02-18 read 2026-09-29; Same-Winners 2026-09-28 read 2026-09-29; Identical Runs 2026-09-27 read 2026-09-29
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: Re-running is near-free (deterministic free minting) so k-repeat reliability is economically viable in a way paid/stateful competitor setups are not
Notes: Adaptive form (recommend k from measured variance) beats a static per-task-type rule; evidence-complete, now blocked only on a product check | 2026-09-29: third independent family (Identical Runs, real coding-agent benchmarking: run-to-run variance exceeds agent-to-agent difference); build caution added from a pass@k-implementation critique (C-0024): k attempts must be genuinely independent full-task rollouts
In plain terms: Show, beside a run's score, how often the agent succeeds every single time (not just once), and suggest running a task a few more times when results are inconsistent or just once when they are stable. Helps you trust a result instead of being fooled by one lucky pass.
What moved: 2026-09-29: +1 source (Identical Runs, 2609.33812); confidence 0.6->0.75; priority 0.80->1.00; evidence-complete pending product check
Why now: A third independent study, this time real-world coding-agent benchmarking, found run-to-run noise exceeds agent-to-agent differences — the case for a reliability readout is now evidence-complete.

Feature: Attribution as a location on the trace + every attribution a routed next action
Pain point: Users cannot tell if a failure is the agent's or the environment's; scores are gameable when isolation is weak
Evidence links: https://github.com/benchjack/benchjack; https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22368; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34177; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.29508; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34262; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35732
Source dates: BenchJack May 2026 read 2026-09-25; HackDetect 2026-07-24 read 2026-09-29; ReplayLens 2026-09-28 + failure-taxonomy 2026-08-26 read 2026-09-29; Unearned Passes 2026-09-28 read 2026-09-29; Failure-Transparent Agents 2026-09-28 read 2026-09-29
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: Env-vs-agent attribution is THE moat asset; now five-plus independent audits prove the failure mode is real, common, and multi-shaped
Notes: Aligns with v3 direction (failures light up in place) but v1-implementable at the scorecard level | 2026-09-29: reinforced by Unearned Passes (ongoing benchmark-maintenance framing) and Failure-Transparent Agents (unsupported success claims as their own attribution category, validating our existing claims-stored-not-trusted design)
In plain terms: When an agent fails, point on the trace to exactly where and why it broke and whether it was the agent's fault or the environment's, with a button to jump straight to fixing it. Turns a confusing failure into a clear next step.
What moved: 2026-09-29: +2 sources (Unearned Passes, Failure-Transparent Agents); confidence 0.6->0.7; priority 0.75->0.875
Why now: Five-plus independent studies now document gameable or mis-attributed agent scores; one directly validates a choice LayerLens already shipped in V1.

Feature: Always show a tradeoff axis (cost or reliability) beside the primary score in comparisons
Pain point: A 1-point accuracy edge can hide a 10x cost difference; single-number rankings mislead
Label: Quick win
Differentiator angle: Extends the shipped refuses-to-average-mismatched-versions guarantee from validity to tradeoff-honesty
Notes: Mostly surfacing data the platform already has (cost measured from real usage); HAL is the reference design
In plain terms: Whenever two runs or models are compared, always show cost (and reliability) right next to the accuracy score, so a tiny accuracy win that actually costs far more is obvious. Stops people picking a winner that is actually a bad deal.
Why now: A small accuracy win can hide a big cost or reliability loss; the leading agent leaderboard (HAL) shows always pairing score with a tradeoff axis.

Feature: Feasibility explanation at task authoring (why is this task not solvable)
Pain point: Authors cannot tell whether a task is solvable or why not; agents waste budget barreling ahead on infeasible tasks
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: LayerLens knows the tools and the answer key so it can compute missing-dependency infeasibility (FeasiGen's masking in reverse)
Notes: Single source; needs a second source or an author-confirmed outcome to reach L1
In plain terms: When someone builds a test task, tell them whether it is actually solvable and, if not, why (for example a tool or record it needs is missing). Saves them from testing agents on impossible tasks.
Why now: Agents waste budget barreling ahead on impossible tasks, but only one source so far, so worth investigating before building.

Feature: Flag same-family judge/agent pairings with a cross-family or Grader suggestion
Pain point: AI judges quietly favor their own model family; verdicts are biased with no visible signal
Source dates: self-preference repo undated read 2026-09-25; identity-conformity 2026-09-27 read 2026-09-29
Label: Proposed
Notes: Upgraded L0->L1 2026-09-29: self-preference now corroborated by an independent 12-model study (C-0014), promoted thesis T-05. Priority jumped 0.90->1.80 (current top item). Cheap to build (metadata comparison + a badge). Next: product check whether Judge vs agent model identity is surfaced today
In plain terms: If the AI grading a result is from the same model family as the agent being graded, show a warning, because judges tend to favor their own family. Keeps a hidden bias from quietly skewing verdicts.
What moved: UP 2026-09-29: priority 0.90->1.80, L0->L1; judge-bias corroborated (C-0014), thesis T-05 promoted
Why now: Cheap to build and now backed by two independent studies that LLM judges favor their own model family; currently the highest priority.

Feature: Confirmations that name the specific record or field that will change
Pain point: Approve/deny gates a risky action but does not inform the decision
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: Field currently answers should-I-ask-permission but not what-to-show-when-asking; open space
Notes: Magentic-UI has the gating tiers; consequence-preview unresolved even for them
In plain terms: Before an agent changes real data, make the confirmation say exactly what will change (which record or field), not just a generic are-you-sure prompt. So people approve knowing the actual consequence.
Why now: The field gates risky actions but does not show their consequences, an open space, though only one source so far.

Feature: Environment lifecycle legibility + checkpoint/branch a run
Pain point: Users cannot see what state an environment keeps across a run, when it stops existing, or cheaply branch/restore a run to try variants
Evidence links: https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22978; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35366; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.33875; https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.14380; https://e2b.dev/resources/build-an-agent-workbench-on-openais-agents-api; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.34313; https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.13672
Source dates: DSec paper 2026-09-19 read 2026-09-29; Planarian 2026-09-28 read 2026-09-29; Counterfactual Rollout Replay 2026-09-27 read 2026-09-29; AgentRewind 2026-08-14 read 2026-09-29 (incomplete access); E2B blog 2026-09-10 read 2026-09-29 (feed summary only); ControlScope 2026-09-28 read 2026-09-29; Recoverability as a System Primitive 2026-09 read 2026-09-29 (incomplete access)
Label: Proposed
Differentiator angle: DSec/Planarian make checkpoint/snapshot/fork a backend or runtime feature from three independent angles; LayerLens's edge is making lifecycle legible and verifiable in the product (deterministic replay as a visible surface)
Notes: Upgraded L0->L1 2026-09-29: two new independent sources (Planarian generalizes to remote state via compensating actions, closest match yet to our own system-type shape; Counterfactual Rollout Replay applies the same primitive to RL training) promote thesis T-06. Dedup: checked vs F-0001..F-0006/F-0009, distinct (lifecycle/state legibility, not reliability readout, attribution, or tool-error guidance). Same-day second update: +3 more sources (AgentRewind, E2B first-party, ControlScope) and a new build caution (Safe to Resume: correct rollback != secure recovery, execution-continuity is a distinct requirement). Same-day third update (pass 3): +1 source (Recoverability as a System Primitive) proposing a governance-layer answer to that exact caution — see idea I-0007.
In plain terms: Make it clear, while someone works in an environment, what information it remembers and when it will shut down, and let them save a checkpoint and branch off to try a variation, choosing how much to change when recovering, and which rule allowed it. Seven independent teams, including a commercial sandbox vendor, already build pieces of this in their backends; the opportunity is to make it visible, understandable, and verifiably safe in the product.
What moved: UP 2026-09-29 (pass 3): +1 source (Recoverability as a System Primitive), now 7 total; proposes a governance-layer answer to the rollback-security risk noted last pass
Why now: Seven converging data points now, one from shipping commercial infrastructure (E2B) not just research, plus a governance-layer design response to the rollback-safety caution that sharpens exactly what 'legible' needs to also mean.

Feature: Establish ground truth for a user-built or prod-imported world (so realistic, free-form environments stay gradeable)
Pain point: A world a user hand-edits or mirrors from prod is realistic but arrives with no answer key, so agents cannot be graded against it deterministically and 'what is correct' is unknown
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: The crux of 'bring your real world and still get verifiable results'; extends answer-key-by-construction to worlds we did not mint (minted worlds use the deterministic grader, imported/edited worlds need ground truth established for actions/state/judge grading)
Notes: Internally derived (Javier + Claude, 2026-09-29), prompted by DSec's stateful/mutable model; not from external research, evidence is our own reasoning plus existing learned-world and actions/state/judge grader capabilities. Dedup: checked vs F-0001..F-0007, distinct (F-0007 = lifecycle/branch; this = ground truth for non-minted worlds). Needs a real user-need signal or external source to leave L0
In plain terms: Let users bring in their real (or freely built) world and still get trustworthy grading, by giving us a way to capture what 'correct' means for that world. Minted worlds come with the right answer built in; imported or edited ones do not, so this is about establishing that ground truth, so people can thoroughly test agents against their actual environment and still trust the verdict.
Why now: Users want to test agents against their real world and still trust the grade; needs a real user signal before building.

Feature: Agent-actionable error and recovery guidance in tool/environment surfaces
Pain point: Tool error messages are written for human developers; agents follow the human-oriented step literally and fail to recover, and more capable agents follow bad steps more, not less
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: Our shipped system types (Salesforce, Linear, SEC EDGAR, Stripe, Gmail) wrap real, human-authored APIs, so this failure mode is a concrete, testable property of our own product surface, not a hypothetical
Notes: New 2026-09-29, from the arXiv inbox's cs.SE harvest. Dedup: checked vs I-0002 (task feasibility) and I-0006 (pre-action confirmations); distinct (post-failure recovery guidance in tool surfaces). Connects to new thesis T-07 (capability amplifies exploitation of flawed interfaces). Needs an internal audit of LayerLens's own tool error surfaces, or a second external source, to reach L1
In plain terms: When a tool call fails, make sure the error message tells the agent something it can actually act on (like which tool to call), not human instructions like 'run this command.' Research found agents, especially more capable ones, follow bad human-oriented advice and fail to recover; naming the right tool call raised recovery from under half to over 80%.
Why now: A concrete, well-evidenced failure mode in exactly the kind of real-API system types LayerLens already ships, with a cheap, testable fix.

Feature: Confidence-scored judge verdicts with escalation on low confidence
Pain point: A Judge's own re-run consistency is a false reassurance of correctness; users have no visible signal of when a verdict is actually uncertain
Source dates: JEV-as-a-Judge 2026-09 read 2026-09-29; jev-harness date unknown read 2026-09-29
Label: Needs evidence
Differentiator angle: A calibrated-confidence, escalate-when-unsure judge pattern is a complementary mitigation to F-0005's same-family flag: F-0005 catches a known bias source, F-0010 catches general judge uncertainty regardless of cause
Notes: New 2026-09-29 (pass 3), from a cross-vendor 'Jev' convergence spotted in the competitor inbox (Arize, Confident AI/DeepEval, Langfuse, Browserbase all covered it the same week). Dedup: checked vs F-0005 (same-family bias flag, different mechanism) and F-0006 (pre-action confirmations, different surface); distinct. Needs a second, independent (non-Jev) source or the product-check result to reach L1.
In plain terms: Show how confident the AI judge actually was in its own verdict, not just pass or fail, and when it wasn't confident, send the case to a stronger judge, a deterministic grader, or a human instead of quietly showing an uncertain verdict as if it were solid.
What moved: NEW 2026-09-29 (pass 3): idea and feature created from the Jev/confidence-cascade research thread
Why now: A fast-moving, already-converging industry pattern (4+ vendors adopted it the same week) that directly answers T-05's 'reproducible but not valid' caution with a concrete, buildable mechanism.
